title: 5 Documentation and Coding Risks in the First 90 Days of FY2027 ICD-10
summary: Explore 5 key ICD-10 coding risks for FY2027, including outdated references, documentation gaps, code selection errors, and compliance best practices.
body_markdown:
## Why the first


90 days


matter for coding compliance


The FY2027 ICD-10-CM code set took effect on October 1, 2026. It applies to patient encounters and discharges from October 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027. Claims with dates of service on or before September 30, 2026, still use the FY2026 codes.


This year’s update is modest. According to the FY2027 ICD-10-CM update, the code set includes 190 new codes, 30 deleted codes, and four revised code titles. Although these changes may appear limited, they can still create implementation challenges. Without reviewing updated coding requirements and providing targeted staff training, healthcare organizations may continue using outdated practices into the new fiscal year.


These are common risks that can take place during an annual code-set transition, not evidence that every organization will experience problems under FY2027. Checking official guidance, educating staff, and tracking recurring errors can help healthcare organizations identify possible errors and strengthen their coding processes.

## 1:


Outdated coding references


The most basic risk is using last year’s code set for this year’s claims. This includes printed manuals, saved code lists, EHR favorites, charge-code mappings, and internal cheat sheets built on FY2026 codes.


When a code is deleted or expanded, an old reference can point coders to a code that is no longer valid or no longer specific. Payer edits may then reject the claim.


The first step is to fix inventory. List every location where a code is stored or recommended, then verify that each reflects the FY2027 Tabular List, Alphabetic Index, and applicable addenda published by


[CMS](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/ICD-10-codes) and the


[CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS).](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Publications/ICD10CM/2027/ICD-10-CM-October-1-2026-FY27-Guidelines.pdf)


## 2: Incomplete clinical documentation


The code is only as strong as the note behind it. When provider documentation is missing, vague, or inconsistent, coders cannot assign the most accurate code. When documentation lacks sufficient detail, coders may assign an appropriate unspecified code or seek clarification from the provider before proceeding.


New codes may provide details, such as laterality, severity, cause, or stage. If providers do not know a new level of detail exists, their notes may not capture it. That gap affects clinical documentation accuracy long before a claim is billed.


In summary, specialty-specific education helps. Show providers which new or expanded codes affect their patients and what the documentation needs to say to support them.


## 3: Incorrect code


selection


Even when documentation is complete, coding errors may still occur. Common causes include:


- Picking a familiar code from memory.


- Selecting the category without assigning the complete code.


- Selecting an unspecified code when the record supports more detail.


Incorrect selection is one of the common ICD-10 coding risks because it can affect medical necessity, risk adjustment, and quality reporting. It also tends to repeat. Repeatedly applying the same coding practice across patient encounters can create a pattern of errors.


Coders should look up codes in the Alphabetic Index and verify them in the Tabular List every time, rather than relying on memory or pick lists alone.


## 4: Missed coding guidelines and sequencing requirements


The ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines for Coding and Reporting sit alongside the code set. They explain conventions, instructional notes such as “code first” and “use additional code,” and the rules for sequencing diagnoses.


The FY2027 guidelines cover October 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027. The official guidelines state that following them when assigning ICD-10-CM codes is required under HIPAA.


Skipping an Excludes note or listing diagnoses in the wrong order can change how a claim is processed. Coding managers should review the FY2027 guideline changes with their teams, not just the new codes.


## 5: Insufficient internal review and staff education


Updates fail quietly when nobody owns them. If changes are not communicated, coders and providers keep working the way they did last year. If no one reviews early claims, the same error can repeat for months.


A light structure is enough to start. Assign an owner for the annual update. Share a summary of changes relevant to each specialty. Then review a sample of early FY2027 claims and denials and turn what you find into targeted education.


## What these risks can mean in practice


None of these risks guarantee a specific outcome. Left unaddressed, though, they may contribute to:


- Claim denials and rework that slow cash flow


- Coder and provider time spent on avoidable queries and corrections


- Findings in internal or external audits


- Inaccurate data for quality reporting and risk adjustment


- Broader compliance exposure if errors form a pattern


## Practical steps to strengthen medical coding compliance


1. **Use official sources:** Download the FY2027 code files, addenda, and Official Guidelines from CMS and CDC NCHS.


2. **Update every reference:** Refresh EHR pick lists, charge mappings, templates, and internal guides.


3. **Educate by specialty:** Give coders and providers short briefings on the changes that affect them.


4. **Clarify queries:** Ensure


documentation queries are clear, compliant, and answered promptly.


5. **Monitor early:** Review denials and a sample of claims from the first 90 days, then audit repeated errors.


6. **Close the loop:** Turn audit findings into updated guidance and follow-up training.


## Keep learning through the code year


Annual updates are easier to manage with a single reference your team can return to. For a deeper look at this year’s changes, see


[CareCloud’s October ICD-10](https://carecloud.com/careclouds-icd-10-plan/) guide for the FY2027 code year


.


## Frequently asked questions


#### When did the FY2027 ICD-10-CM codes take effect?


The FY2027 ICD-10-CM code set took effect on October 1, 2026. It applies to patient encounters and discharges from October 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027. Claims with dates of service on or before September 30, 2026, should continue to use FY2026 codes. Organizations should confirm their systems apply the correct code set by date of service.


#### How many codes


changed


in the FY2027 ICD-10-CM update?


According to the summary published with the official addenda, the FY2027 update adds 190 new ICD-10-CM codes,


deletes


30, and revises 4. Many deletions reflect codes expanded into more specific subcategories. Teams should review the full addenda from CDC NCHS, since changes to instructional notes and code titles also matter for


accurate


coding.


#### What is coding compliance in healthcare?


Coding compliance means assigning diagnosis and procedure codes that accurately reflect the medical record and follow official code sets, conventions, and guidelines. It depends on complete clinical documentation, current references, trained staff, and regular internal review.


Effective coding compliance promotes claim accuracy and data reliability, but it does not


eliminate


the possibility of an audit.

#### Where can I find the official FY2027 ICD-10-CM guidelines?


The FY2027 ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines for Coding and Reporting are published by the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics and linked from the CMS ICD-10 webpage. They are approved by the four Cooperating Parties: AHA, AHIMA, CMS, and NCHS. Use them alongside the FY2027 tabular list, index, and addenda when coding
